text: Lesson seventeen showed you the mechanism: a small, deliberate perturbation that pushes a correctly classified input across a model's decision boundary. This lesson points that same mechanism at something a security team actually relies on — a model built to catch bad behavior. When that happens, it has a specific name: an evasion attack.

An evasion attack targets a classifier that's already deployed and already making real decisions — a malware scanner, a spam filter, a network intrusion detector — and it has one goal: get a malicious input past that model at inference time. Pull that off against a malware scanner, and a file that should have been quarantined gets delivered instead. Pull it off against a spam filter, and a phishing email lands in an inbox.

Here's what makes this harder than perturbing a photo. A modified malware file still has to run and still has to carry its payload, so an attacker can't just add arbitrary noise the way you can to pixel values. Researchers describe this as the gap between a feature-space attack, which perturbs the numbers a model sees, and a problem-space attack, which has to perturb the real file while keeping it functional — padding bytes, unused code sections, changes that don't break what the malware does.

Text classifiers face their own version of the same constraint. Published research on evading spam and phishing filters describes the good word attack: inserting or substituting words and characters the filter's training data associates with legitimate mail, diluting its detection signal without breaking the message's ability to actually phish its target. None of that requires touching the model's weights — only an understanding of what its decision depends on.

The lesson underneath all of this is a reframing: any classifier your organization relies on for detection is part of the attack surface, not just part of the defense. An adaptive adversary will probe its decision boundary the way they'd probe a firewall rule set. Next, we look at what real defenses buy you — and what each one costs.
